To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

young Lebanese-Canadian Christian women construct the “ideal” and “healthy” body as a thin body, which they view as their sole responsibility to achieve, and they engage in a variety of disciplinary bodily practices to attain it.

young Lebanese-Canadian Christian women are exposed to multiple discourses about health and obesity, and that these discourses are internalized and re-produced in their everyday lives in ways that may be harmful.

young Christian Lebanese- Canadian women construct themselves as neoliberal and poststructuralist subjects within the context of a dominant obesity discourse, which is replete with contradictory messages.
In summary, our research is concerned with
how young women construct their subjectivities in relation to the body, “health” practices, and the obesity discourse, and the impacts of their hybrid cultural identities on their constructions.

the ways in which the young women’s hybrid cultural identity, the discourses of obesity, and the discourses of health intersect and impact their constructions of the body, health, and health practices.

the young Christian Lebanese women’s discursive construction of their bodies, health, and health practices, which are shaped by their hybrid cultural identities as well as their diasporic spaces and their multiple subject positions.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the participants’ constructions of “healthy” bodies and “health”/“healthy” practices reflect the complex ways in which they are positioned within various discourses.

the young Lebanese-Canadian Christian women in our study have been socialized into a culture of “health” that is largely informed by the dominant neoliberal discourse of obesity, and that they have internalized the “docile” and “ideal” body.
these young women’s discursive constructions of health and the body reveal the complex and contradictory ways in which they negotiate the dominant neoliberal discourse of “obesity” and the body.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the participants’ discursive constructions of their body and “health practices” are influenced by their hybrid cultural identities, and that these constructions are also shaped by their diasporic spaces.

the young Christian Lebanese women’s constructions of their bodies and “health” are shaped by their hybrid cultural identities, diasporic spaces, and their awareness of and resistance to dominant discourses.
the Lebanese-Canadian women are not simply passive subjects who are “judged by their covers” but rather active agents in the production of discourses surrounding health and the body.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the Lebanese-Canadian young women’s hybrid cultural and diasporic identities, as well as their positioning in relation to the dominant discourses surrounding health and the body, shape their constructions of the body, and “health” and “healthy” bodily practices.
the young Christian Lebanese women are not passive recipients of dominant obesity discourse.

, despite their awareness of the dominant discourses on health, obesity, the body, and beauty, the young Christian Lebanese women in this study are still susceptible to the neoliberal discourse of self-responsibility for “health.”
